translation: The Bi Lun states: "The yin qi — in stillness the spirit is stored; in agitation it is extinguished; when food and drink are doubled by oneself, the intestines and stomach are thereby injured." This is speaking comprehensively of it. Dividing it into two: drink and food. And the Classic states: "Thus, in great drinking, qi then rebels; thus, in satiety eating, the sinews and vessels become transverse and slack, then intestinal prolapse becomes hemorrhoids." Drink is the qi without form; when [it is] injured, one should induce sweating and promote urination, so that above and below separately disperse its dampness — [the medicaments] such as [Ge Hua] Jie Xing Tang and Wu Ling San govern. Food is a thing with form; when [it is] injured, one should deplete its grain, and next best nothing surpasses dispersing and guiding — [the medicaments] such as Ding Xiang Lan Fan Wan and Zhi Zhu Wan govern. Somewhat severe, then attack and transform — [the medicaments] such as San Leng Xiao Ji Wan and Mu Xiang Jian Xian Wan govern. The most severe, then either vomit or drain — [the medicaments] such as Gua Di San and Bei Ji Wan govern. Taking leveling as the criterion. Because the spleen is already injured and moreover, with the medicament injuring [it], the circulating transporting qi is reduced and pared, and the food becomes all the harder to digest. Hence the Wu Chang Zheng Lun states: "In treating disease with great poison, [one] removes six of ten; treating disease with ordinary poison, [one] removes seven of ten; treating disease with minor poison, [one] removes eight of ten; treating disease with no poison, [one] removes nine of ten. With grain, flesh, fruit, and vegetables, one nourishes and exhausts it; do not let [the treatment] exceed [this], wounding the orthopathic [qi]. If it is not completely carried out, repeat it again, as in the law." The sage, holding up this stern warning, makes it a blessing for ten thousand generations. If one is able to be cautious in speech and temperate in food and drink, this is what is called 'treating the not-yet-diseased.'
